title: The virtuous elephant
hook: an elephant rescues a lost man, who comes back to saw off his tusks (Jataka 72)
tomorrow: The fish who prayed for rain

segments.voice: Yesterday: the monkey gardeners, so conscientious they pulled up every sapling. Your line: don't pull up the roots. Today, kindness that keeps going after it's been betrayed.

A man from Benares has gone into the forest for work and lost his way. He wanders, crying out in fear. Then a huge white elephant steps out of the trees. The man runs. The elephant stops. The man stops. The elephant steps forward; the man runs again. At last the man understands: this animal means no harm. He's the bodhisatta, the tale says, and he's come to help.
screen: `A MAN LOST IN THE FOREST.` → `A WHITE ELEPHANT APPEARS.` → `HE COMES TO HELP.`

segments.voice: First, the rescue. The elephant takes the man home, feeds him on fruit, and carries him on his back out of the forest to the road. But as they go, the man quietly notes every tree and hill along the way. Second, the bargain. Back in Benares, he walks down the street of the ivory carvers and asks what they'd pay for the tusks of a living elephant. A lot, they say. So he takes a saw and goes back. Third, the gift. He tells the elephant he's poor, with nothing to live on. Would he give him his tusks? The elephant kneels and lets him saw. He gives them freely, saying it isn't that he doesn't value them: the wisdom he is seeking is dearer to him. The man sells them, then comes back for the stumps. The elephant gives those too. Then he comes a third time and digs out the roots of the tusks. Each time, the elephant lets him. Fourth, the end. As the man walks away, the tale says, the earth splits open and swallows him. A tree spirit speaks a verse: give an ungrateful man the whole world, and it still won't satisfy him. The tale never calls the elephant foolish. He gives three times, each gift costing more, and the tale saves its judgment for the taker. The man's ingratitude doesn't get to decide who the elephant is. The tale's last line names the man as Devadatta, whose ingratitude toward the Buddha is the story's frame.
screen: `CARRIED OUT OF THE FOREST.` · `THE STREET OF THE IVORY CARVERS.` · `TUSKS, THEN STUMPS, THEN ROOTS.` · `THE EARTH OPENS.` · then, large: `GOOD TO THE UNGRATEFUL.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone took your help and gave nothing back; not the deepest wound you carry, a small one. Forgiving isn't approving, so just see if you can set the weight of it down for a moment, the way the elephant knelt. Breathe out, and let your kindness belong to you, not to them.
Sila. Virtue, good conduct: what the virtuous elephant showed, rescuing a lost man, then giving him tusks, stumps and roots, and staying good to the end. Today's word.

Your line: good to the ungrateful. The week in lines: dig once more, from a dead mouse, the dance cost him, honor the eldest, the crab remembers, don't pull up the roots. Day eight hundred twenty-six, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Silavanaga Jataka as a picture of generosity and patience that don't depend on gratitude, and as a warning about where ingratitude leads.

fork.setup: you're the elephant. the man you carried out of the forest is back with a saw, asking for your tusks. what do you do?
options: drive him off. you saved his life once already.
kneel and let him take them.

fork.reveal: the elephant kneels and lets him saw, saying the wisdom he seeks is dearer to him than tusks, and gives again each time he returns.

original.note: Pali sila: virtue, good conduct. the tale's name, Silavanaga, means the virtuous elephant.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad story about a greedy man.
what it means: the elephant stays generous even while he's being used, and the ungrateful man is never satisfied.

what a scholar hears: the tale's last line names the man as Devadatta, so it's told in the frame of Devadatta's ingratitude toward the Buddha; the elephant practices the perfections of generosity and patience.
recall: going out, like a lamp's flame

chat.says: Was the elephant foolish to keep giving to a man who kept taking?
options: The tale never calls him foolish; it saves its judgment for the taker.
Yes, the tale's lesson is that kindness to takers is always wasted.
Yes, and the tree spirit scolds the elephant in the final verse.
chat.meaning: He gave three times, each gift costing more. The verse judges the ungrateful man, and the man's ingratitude doesn't decide who the elephant is.

Benares.meaning: the city the lost man comes from

bodhisatta.meaning: the future Buddha, in a past life

Devadatta.meaning: the man in this tale, ungrateful toward the Buddha

notes: Confirm details of Jataka 72: a Benares forester lost and lamenting; the white elephant (bodhisatta) approaches, the man runs and stops in turn; the elephant feeds him and carries him out; the man notes landmarks; ivory workers would buy living elephant's tusks; the elephant kneels and gives tusks, then the stumps, then the roots; the earth opens and swallows the man; a tree spirit's verse about the ungrateful never being satisfied; the man identified as Devadatta.
'He knows the man is taking advantage; the text says so' should be checked against the Pali; soften to 'the tale suggests' if not explicit.
Original: सील (sila); the title gloss 'the virtuous elephant' is the index title's rendering, not an etymology claim. Confirm the Devanagari spelling.

Devadatta is named as the tale names him; Keeper to confirm the framing is fair.

Editor pass: cut 'for days'; replaced 'asks only that the man treat this gift well' with the elephant's stated reason (the wisdom he seeks is dearer than the tusks); removed the unverified claim that the text says he knew he was being used (teach, myth, trapdoor); cut 'cousin' to keep to what the tale says; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.

Audit pass: practice no longer claims the elephant 'didn't approve' (the tale says nothing of it). Confirmed in Chalmers: the man asked for 'a bit' of tusk, came back for stumps then roots, the earth opened; Devadatta frame at the Bamboo-grove.
